User Input / Output:
Read input from standard input and write to standard output. Read an integer n and print it back.

Example: Input 5 → Output 5
Data Types: Review primitive data types and their ranges. Declare an int, long long, float, double and char; read one value of each and print them back.
If Else statements:
Given an integer n, print Positive, Negative or Zero using if-else.

Example: n = -4 → Negative
Switch Statement:
Given a number from 1 to 7, print the corresponding day of the week using a switch statement.

Example: 3 → Wednesday
What are arrays, strings?: Declare an array of n integers and a string, read them, then print the array in reverse and the length of the string.
For loops:
Using a for loop, print all numbers from 1 to n and then their sum.

Example: n = 5 → 1 2 3 4 5, sum 15
While loops:
Using a while loop, print the digits of an integer n from last to first.

Example: n = 472 → 2 7 4
Functions (Pass by Reference and Value): Write a swap(a, b) that swaps two numbers using pass-by-reference, and one that attempts it by value — observe why only the reference version changes the caller's variables.
Time Complexity [Learn Basics, and then:
Learn Big-O notation. For each snippet (single loop, nested loops, halving loop), state its time complexity.

Example: two nested loops over n → O(n^2)
Patterns:
Given n, print a right-angled triangle of stars with n rows.

Example: n = 3 → row1 *, row2 **, row3 ***
C++ STL: Practice the STL: create a vector, pair, map and set. Read n numbers and print the distinct ones in sorted order using a set.
Java Collections: Practice Java Collections: use ArrayList, HashMap and TreeSet. Read n numbers and print the distinct ones in sorted order using a TreeSet.
Count Digits:
Given an integer n, count the number of digits in it.

Example: n = 7789 → 4
GCD Or HCF:
Given two integers a and b, find their greatest common divisor (GCD).

Example: a = 12, b = 18 → 6
Print all Divisors:
Given an integer n, print all of its divisors in increasing order.

Example: n = 12 → 1 2 3 4 6 12
Check for Prime:
Given an integer n, determine whether it is prime.

Example: n = 13 → true
Understand recursion by print something: Using recursion (no loops), print the word Hello exactly n times.
Print name N times using recursion: Given a name and n, print the name n times using recursion.
Print 1 to N using recursion:
Given n, print numbers from 1 to n using recursion.

Example: n = 4 → 1 2 3 4
Print N to 1 using recursion:
Given n, print numbers from n down to 1 using recursion.

Example: n = 4 → 4 3 2 1
Sum of first N numbers:
Given n, return the sum 1 + 2 + ... + n (try it with recursion).

Example: n = 5 → 15
Reverse an array:
Given an array, reverse it in place.

Example: [1,2,3,4] → [4,3,2,1]
Hashing Theory: Learn hashing: precompute frequencies for O(1) lookups. Task: given an array and queries, answer each query's frequency using a hash map.
Counting frequencies of array elements:
Given an array, print each distinct element with how many times it occurs.

Example: [10,5,10,15,10,5] → 10→3, 5→2, 15→1
Selection Sort:
Sort an array in ascending order using Selection Sort (repeatedly select the minimum of the unsorted part and place it next).

Example: [13,46,24,52,20,9] → [9,13,20,24,46,52]
Bubble Sort: Sort an array using Bubble Sort (repeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order elements so the largest bubbles to the end).
Insertion Sort: Sort an array using Insertion Sort (insert each element into its correct position within the sorted prefix).
Merge Sort: Sort an array using Merge Sort (divide into halves, sort each, merge). Time O(n log n).
Recursive Bubble Sort: Implement Bubble Sort recursively instead of with nested loops.
Quick Sort: Sort an array using Quick Sort (choose a pivot, partition smaller/larger, recurse on each side).
Largest Element in an Array:
Return the largest element of an array.

Example: [2,5,1,3,0] → 5
Second Largest Element in an Array witho:
Find the second-largest element in a single pass, without sorting.

Example: [1,2,4,7,7,5] → 5
Linear Search: Given an array and a target, return the index of the target (or -1) using linear search.
Find the Union:
Given two sorted arrays, return their union: all distinct elements in sorted order.

Example: [1,2,3,4,5] & [2,3,4,4,5] → [1,2,3,4,5]
Longest subarray with given sum K(positi:
Given an array of positive numbers and a target K, return the length of the longest subarray summing to K.

Example: [1,2,3,1,1,1,1], K=3 → 3
Longest subarray with sum K (Positives +: Same as before but the array may contain negatives and zero. Use a prefix-sum hash map.
Print subarray with maximum subarray sum:
Find the contiguous subarray with the maximum sum (Kadane's) and print the subarray itself.

Example: [-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4] → [4,-1,2,1] (sum 6)
Leaders in an Array problem:
An element is a leader if it is greater than every element to its right. Print all leaders.

Example: [10,22,12,3,0,6] → [22,12,6]
Largest Subarray with 0 Sum:
Return the length of the longest subarray whose elements sum to 0.

Example: [15,-2,2,-8,1,7,10,23] → 5
Count number of subarrays with given xor: Given an array and K, count subarrays whose XOR equals K (use prefix-XOR with a hash map).
Find the repeating and missing number:
An array of size n holds numbers 1..n with one repeating and one missing. Find both.

Example: [3,1,2,5,3] → repeating 3, missing 4
Count Inversions:
Count pairs (i, j) with i < j and a[i] > a[j] (use a modified Merge Sort).

Example: [5,3,2,1,4] → 8
Implement Lower Bound: In a sorted array, return the first index whose value is ≥ target (the lower bound).
Implement Upper Bound: In a sorted array, return the first index whose value is > target (the upper bound).
Floor/Ceil in Sorted Array: Given a sorted array and x, find the floor (largest value ≤ x) and the ceil (smallest value ≥ x).
Count occurrences of a number in a sorte: Count how many times a target appears in a sorted array using first and last occurrence (binary search).
Find out how many times has an array bee: A sorted array was rotated; return the number of rotations (= index of the minimum element).
Find square root of a number in log n:
Given n, return the integer part of its square root using binary search.

Example: n = 28 → 5
Find the Nth root of a number using bina: Given m and n, return the integer nth root of m, or -1 if m is not a perfect nth power, using binary search.
Aggressive Cows: Place k cows in given stall positions to maximize the minimum distance between any two cows. Binary search on the answer.
Book Allocation Problem: Allocate books (page counts) contiguously to m students so the maximum pages assigned to a student is minimized. Binary search on the answer.
Painter's partition: Divide boards among k painters (each takes a contiguous block) to minimize the maximum time. Binary search on the answer.
Kth element of 2 sorted arrays: Given two sorted arrays, return the kth smallest element of their merged order.
Find the row with maximum number of 1's: In a row-wise sorted binary matrix, return the index of the row containing the most 1s.
Matrix Median: Find the median of a row-wise sorted matrix with an odd number of elements (binary search on the value).
Count Number of Substrings: Given a string and an integer k, count the number of substrings that contain exactly k distinct characters.
Introduction to LinkedList, learn about: Define a singly linked-list node (a value plus a next pointer). Build a list from an array and print it.
Inserting a node in LinkedList: Insert a node with a given value at a given position (head, tail, or index) in a singly linked list.
Find the length of the linkedlist [learn: Return the number of nodes in a singly linked list by traversing it.
Search an element in the LL: Return true if a given value exists in the linked list, else false.
Introduction to DLL, learn about struct,: Define a doubly linked-list node (prev, value, next). Build a DLL from an array and print it forward.
Insert a node in DLL: Insert a node at a given position in a doubly linked list, fixing the prev/next pointers of neighbours.
Delete a node in DLL: Delete the node at a given position in a doubly linked list.
Reverse a DLL: Reverse a doubly linked list in place by swapping each node's prev and next pointers.
Length of Loop in LL: If the linked list contains a cycle, return the number of nodes in the loop, else 0 (Floyd's algorithm).
Sort a LL of 0's 1's and 2's by changing: Given a linked list of values 0, 1 and 2, sort it by rearranging links (not by overwriting values).
Add 1 to a number represented by LL:
A number's digits are stored in a linked list (head = most significant). Add 1 and return the resulting list.

Example: 1→9→9 → 2→0→0
Delete all occurrences of a key in DLL: Delete every node equal to a given key in a doubly linked list.
Find pairs with given sum in DLL: Given a sorted doubly linked list and a target, return all pairs of values that sum to the target.
Remove duplicates from sorted DLL: Remove duplicate values from a sorted doubly linked list so each value appears once.
Flattening of LL: Each node has a next pointer and a sorted child (bottom) list. Flatten everything into a single sorted list.
Sort a stack using recursion: Sort a stack in ascending order using only recursion (no extra data structures).
Generate all binary strings: Given n, generate all binary strings of length n that have no two consecutive 1s.
Learn All Patterns of Subsequences (Theo:
Learn the pick / not-pick recursion pattern. Task: print all subsequences of an array.

Example: [3,1,2] → [], [3], [1], [2], [3,1], [3,2], [1,2], [3,1,2]
Count all subsequences with sum K: Count the number of subsequences of an array whose elements sum to K.
Check if there exists a subsequence with: Return true if some subsequence of the array sums to K.
Subset Sum-I:
Return the sorted list of all possible subset sums of an array.

Example: [2,3] → [0,2,3,5]
Rat in a Maze: In an n×n grid (1 = open, 0 = blocked), find all paths from the top-left to the bottom-right moving Down/Left/Right/Up, given as direction strings.
M Coloring Problem: Given a graph and m colors, determine whether the graph can be colored so that no two adjacent vertices share a color.
Introduction to Bit Manipulation [Theory: Learn the bitwise operators (AND, OR, XOR, shifts). Task: print the binary representation of a number, then convert a binary string back to a number.
Check if the i-th bit is set or not:
Given n and i, return whether the i-th bit (0-indexed) of n is set.

Example: n = 13 (1101), i = 2 → true
Check if a number is odd or not: Using bit manipulation, determine whether n is odd (check n & 1).
Count the number of set bits:
Return the number of set bits (1s) in the binary representation of n.

Example: n = 13 → 3
Set/Unset the rightmost unset bit:
Given n, set its rightmost 0 bit to 1 and return the result.

Example: n = 11 (1011) → 15 (1111)
Swap two numbers: Swap two integers without using a temporary variable (use XOR).
Find xor of numbers from L to R: Return the XOR of all integers in the range [L, R].
Find the two numbers appearing odd numbe: In an array where exactly two numbers occur an odd number of times (the rest occur an even number of times), find those two numbers.
Print Prime Factors of a Number:
Print all prime factors of n.

Example: n = 60 → 2 2 3 5
All Divisors of a Number:
Print all divisors of n in O(sqrt(n)).

Example: n = 36 → 1 2 3 4 6 9 12 18 36
Find Prime Factorisation of a Number usi: Precompute the smallest prime factor for every number with a sieve, then answer prime-factorisation queries in O(log n).
Implement Stack using Arrays: Implement a stack (push, pop, top, size) backed by an array.
Implement Queue using Arrays: Implement a queue (enqueue, dequeue, front, size) backed by a circular array.
Implement stack using Linkedlist: Implement a stack using a singly linked list.
Implement queue using Linkedlist: Implement a queue using a singly linked list with head and tail pointers.
Infix to Postfix Conversion using Stack:
Convert an infix expression to postfix using a stack and operator precedence.

Example: a+b*c → abc*+
Next Smaller Element: For each element, find the next smaller element to its right (or -1) using a monotonic stack.
Number of NGEs to the right: For each query index, count how many next-greater elements lie to its right.
Fruit Into Baskets:
Given fruit types in a row, find the longest contiguous subarray containing at most 2 distinct types (sliding window).

Example: [1,2,1,2,3] → 4
Introduction to Priority Queues using Bi: Learn how a binary heap backs a priority queue. Task: insert n numbers into a max-heap and pop them all to print in descending order.
Min Heap and Max Heap Implementation: Implement a min-heap and a max-heap supporting insert and extract-min / extract-max.
Check if an array represents a min-heap: Given an array, return whether it satisfies the min-heap property (every parent ≤ its children).
Convert min Heap to max Heap: Given an array that is a valid min-heap, convert it into a max-heap in place.
Kth smallest element in an array [use pr:
Return the kth smallest element of an array using a heap.

Example: [7,10,4,3,20,15], k=3 → 7
Sort K sorted array: Sort a nearly-sorted array where each element is at most k positions from its final spot, using a min-heap.
Replace each array element by its corres:
Replace each element with its rank (1-based) among the distinct sorted values.

Example: [20,15,26,2,98,6] → [4,3,5,1,6,2]
Connect `n` ropes with minimal cost:
Repeatedly join the two shortest ropes (cost = their sum) until one remains; return the minimum total cost.

Example: [4,3,2,6] → 29
Maximum Sum Combination: Given two arrays and k, return the k largest sums formed by picking one element from each array.
Fractional Knapsack Problem: Maximize value carried in a knapsack of capacity W where items may be taken fractionally (greedy by value/weight ratio).
Greedy algorithm to find minimum number:
Given coin denominations and an amount, return the minimum number of coins (greedy works for canonical systems).

Example: amount 49 → 5
N meetings in one room: Given start and end times, select the maximum number of non-overlapping meetings for a single room.
Minimum number of platforms required for: Given train arrival and departure times, find the minimum number of platforms so that no train waits.
Job sequencing Problem: Each job has a deadline and a profit and takes unit time. Schedule jobs to maximize total profit.
Program for Shortest Job First (or SJF): Given CPU burst times, compute the average waiting time under non-preemptive Shortest-Job-First scheduling.
Program for Least Recently Used (LRU) Pa: Given a page-reference sequence and a cache capacity, count the page faults using the LRU replacement policy.
Introduction to Trees: Learn tree terminology (root, child, leaf, height). Task: given a binary tree, count its total nodes and its leaves.
Binary Tree Representation in C++: Define a binary-tree node in C++ (value, left, right), build a small tree, and print the root and its children.
Binary Tree Representation in Java: Define a binary-tree node in Java, build a small tree, and print the root and its children.
Binary Tree Traversals in Binary Tree: Given a binary tree, return its preorder, inorder and postorder traversals.
Preorder, Inorder, and Postorder Travers: Compute all three DFS traversals of a binary tree in a single pass using an explicit state stack.
Top View of Binary Tree: Return the top view of a binary tree (the nodes visible from above, ordered by horizontal distance).
Bottom View of Binary Tree: Return the bottom view of a binary tree (the nodes visible from below, ordered by horizontal distance).
Root to Node Path in Binary Tree: Given a target value, return the path of node values from the root to that node.
Check for Children Sum Property: Check whether every node's value equals the sum of its children's values (treat a missing child as 0).
Minimum time taken to BURN the Binary Tr: A fire starts at a given node and spreads to adjacent nodes each minute. Return the time to burn the whole tree.
Requirements needed to construct a Uniqu: Learn which pairs of traversals uniquely determine a binary tree. Task: given inorder + preorder, state whether the tree is unique and why.
Introduction to Binary Search Tree: Learn the BST property (left subtree < node < right subtree). Task: search for a value in a BST and return true/false.
Find Min/Max in BST: Return the minimum and maximum values in a binary search tree.
Ceil in a Binary Search Tree: Return the smallest value ≥ x in a BST (its ceil), or -1 if none exists.
Floor in a Binary Search Tree: Return the largest value ≤ x in a BST (its floor), or -1 if none exists.
Largest BST in Binary Tree: Return the size (number of nodes) of the largest subtree that is itself a valid BST.
Graph and Types: Learn graph types (directed/undirected, weighted/unweighted). Task: given edges, build an adjacency list and print each node's neighbours.
Graph Representation | C++: Represent a graph as an adjacency list in C++ from a given list of edges.
Graph Representation | Java: Represent a graph as an adjacency list in Java from a given list of edges.
BFS: Return the Breadth-First Search traversal order of a graph starting from node 0.
DFS: Return the Depth-First Search traversal order of a graph starting from node 0.
Connected Components Problem in Matrix: Count the number of connected components (groups of connected 1s) in a grid.
Cycle Detection in Undirected Graph (bfs: Detect whether an undirected graph contains a cycle using BFS.
Cycle Detection in Undirected Graph (dfs: Detect whether an undirected graph contains a cycle using DFS.
Topo Sort: Return a topological ordering of a directed acyclic graph (DFS-based).
Kahn's Algorithm: Return a topological ordering of a DAG using Kahn's BFS (indegree) algorithm.
Cycle Detection in Directed Graph (BFS): Detect a cycle in a directed graph: it has one if Kahn's algorithm cannot order all nodes.
Shortest Path in UG with unit weights: Return the shortest distances from a source in an unweighted undirected graph using BFS.
Shortest Path in DAG: Return the shortest distances from a source in a weighted DAG using topological order.
Djisktra's Algorithm: Return the shortest distances from a source in a graph with non-negative edge weights using Dijkstra's algorithm.
Why priority Queue is used in Djisktra's: Understand why a min-priority-queue makes Dijkstra efficient. Task: implement Dijkstra using a priority queue.
Minimum steps to reach end from start by: From a start number, reach a target by repeatedly multiplying by an array element and taking mod 100000. Return the minimum number of steps (BFS over states).
Bellman Ford Algorithm: Return the shortest distances from a source allowing negative edges, and report if a negative cycle exists (Bellman-Ford).
Floyd Warshal Algorithm: Return all-pairs shortest path distances using the Floyd-Warshall algorithm.
Minimum Spanning Tree: Learn what an MST is. Task: return the total weight of a minimum spanning tree of a weighted undirected graph.
Prim's Algorithm: Return the weight of the minimum spanning tree using Prim's algorithm.
Disjoint Set [Union by Rank]: Implement a Disjoint Set Union with union by rank and path compression; support find and union.
Disjoint Set [Union by Size]: Implement a Disjoint Set Union with union by size and path compression.
Kruskal's Algorithm: Return the MST weight using Kruskal's algorithm (sort edges, then union with DSU).
Articulation Point: Find all articulation points (cut vertices) of an undirected graph.
Kosaraju's Algorithm: Count the number of strongly connected components of a directed graph using Kosaraju's algorithm.
Dynamic Programming Introduction: Learn memoization vs tabulation. Task: compute the nth Fibonacci number with both top-down and bottom-up DP.
Frog Jump(DP-3): A frog on stair 0 can jump 1 or 2 steps; the cost of a jump is the absolute height difference. Return the minimum cost to reach stair n-1.
Frog Jump with k distances(DP-4): As above, but the frog may jump up to k steps. Return the minimum total cost.
Ninja's Training (DP 7): Over n days pick one of 3 activities per day without repeating the previous day's activity; maximize total merit points.
3-d DP : Ninja and his friends (DP-13): Two players move top to bottom in a grid (diagonal moves allowed) collecting chocolates; maximize the combined total without double-counting shared cells.
Subset sum equal to target (DP- 14): Return whether some subset of the array sums exactly to the target.
Count Subsets with Sum K (DP - 17): Count the number of subsets whose elements sum to K.
Count Partitions with Given Difference (: Count the ways to split the array into two subsets whose sums differ by exactly D.
Unbounded Knapsack (DP - 23): Maximize value within capacity W where each item can be used any number of times.
Rod Cutting Problem | (DP - 24): Given prices for rod lengths 1..n, cut a rod of length n into pieces to maximize total price.
Print Longest Common Subsequence | (DP -:
Given two strings, print their longest common subsequence.

Example: abcde, ace → ace
Longest Common Substring | (DP - 27): Return the length of the longest common substring (contiguous) of two strings.
Printing Longest Increasing Subsequence|: Print a longest strictly increasing subsequence of an array.
Longest Increasing Subsequence |(DP-43):
Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.

Example: [10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18] → 4
Longest Bitonic Subsequence |(DP-46): Return the length of the longest subsequence that first strictly increases, then strictly decreases.
Matrix Chain Multiplication|(DP-48): Given matrix dimensions, find the minimum number of scalar multiplications to multiply the whole chain (memoization).
Matrix Chain Multiplication | Bottom-Up|: Solve Matrix Chain Multiplication using bottom-up tabulation.
Longest String with All Prefixes: Among the given words, return the longest word such that every one of its prefixes is also present in the list.
Number of Distinct Substrings in a Strin: Return the number of distinct substrings of a string (insert all suffixes into a trie).
Bit PreRequisites for TRIE Problems: Learn to store numbers bit-by-bit in a binary trie. Task: insert numbers into a binary trie, then for a query x find the maximum XOR of x with any inserted number.
Hashing In Strings | Theory: Learn string (prefix) hashing for O(1) substring comparison. Task: given a string and queries, compare two substrings for equality using prefix hashes.
Count palindromic subsequence in given s: Count the number of palindromic subsequences in a string using dynamic programming.
